analysis.one_liner: Lets Camp Lejeune water-contamination victims sue the federal government for damages.
analysis.headline: The bill died in House committee without a hearing or a vote, though its aims were later folded into the PACT Act signed in August 2022.
analysis.plain_summary: Between 1953 and 1987, the water supply at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune in North Carolina was contaminated. This bill would have let anyone who lived, worked, or was otherwise exposed there for at least 30 days — including family members and babies exposed before birth — sue the federal government for damages in federal court. It would have stopped the government from using an immunity defense to get those lawsuits thrown out, set a two-year window to file, and barred punitive damages and duplicate lawsuits. The bill never received a hearing or a vote; similar language became law in 2022 as part of the separate PACT Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Veterans, their family members, civilian workers, and children exposed in utero who were harmed by Camp Lejeune's contaminated water between 1953 and 1987. For decades they had no way to sue the government; this bill would have opened the federal courthouse to them, waived the government's immunity defense, and let them prove causation on an "at least as likely as not" standard.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Camp Lejeune water-contamination victims and families

how_it_helps.text: It created a right to sue in federal court for anyone — veterans, family members, civilian workers, and children exposed before birth — who spent at least 30 days at Camp Lejeune between August 1953 and December 1987.

It stripped the government of an immunity defense it could otherwise use to get such lawsuits dismissed, and used a relaxed 'at least as likely as not' standard of proof for showing the water caused the harm.
It barred other statutes of limitations from applying and set a two-year filing window, giving long-delayed claimants a realistic chance to bring cases.

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Treasury — the government would have paid damages for harms caused by its own water system. No private industry bore the cost directly, and awards would have been offset by VA, Medicare, and Medicaid benefits already paid for the same harm.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, via government damage awards

drawbacks.text: Damages would have been offset by any VA disability, Medicare, or Medicaid payments related to the exposure, so people already receiving benefits would recover less than their full harm.
No punitive damages would have been allowed, and all claims would have funneled through a single federal court in eastern North Carolina, raising the prospect of delay for large numbers of claimants.
Claimants had only two years after enactment to file, a short window for illnesses that can take decades to surface.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a genuine injustice — poisoning of Marines, families, and civilian workers by their own government, with no remedy — and its main cost would have fallen on the Treasury, not on ordinary people. Its limits: awards offset by existing benefits, no punitive damages, and a single venue for hundreds of thousands of potential claims. On balance a strong, narrowly targeted remedy whose main drawback was dying in committee without ever being considered.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the Camp Lejeune Justice Act of 2022 on January 25, 2022, with bipartisan cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day and never received a markup or floor vote.
On November 1, 2022 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, where it remained when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
It had 17 cosponsors split between 6 Democrats and 11 Republicans, showing bipartisan interest that did not translate into action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal government, which kept the immunity defense the bill would have stripped and faced no damages from this bill — though Congress later enacted substantially similar relief in the PACT Act.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal government, which faced no damages

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship in the House.

for.name: 17 House cosponsors (6 Democrats, 11 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred in January 2022, and sent it to subcommittee in November 2022, where it died.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split across both parties, 6 Democrats and 11 Republicans, and there was no recorded opposition vote — the bill died quietly in committee rather than in a partisan fight.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped a key immunity defense and exposed the government to damage awards for the contamination; the government also avoided this exposure as long as the bill stayed in committee.
A new federal cause of action would have generated large volumes of contingency-fee litigation; nothing reached a vote, so no gains materialized from this bill.
